summary:
Section 198 of Brunei's Syariah Penal Code Order 2013 creates the trans-specific offence of "a man posing as a woman or vice versa", punishable where the conduct is deemed without reasonable excuse or committed for immoral purposes. Official guidance on the code states that it binds all persons present in the country, including tourists, and travel agents have been briefed to that effect.

Human Rights Watch's #OUTLAWED survey places Brunei among at least two countries, with Oman, whose national laws expressly criminalise "posing as" or "imitating" a person of a different sex. Malaysia is recorded as having a state-sharia analogue to the offence.

Cross-dressing has been prosecuted. On 11 March 2015 a civil servant was fined B$1,000 under the Syariah Penal Code Order for cross-dressing, the one documented conviction known to be recorded against the provision.

The US State Department's 2017 report on human rights practices describes the code as banning men from dressing as women and women from dressing as men "without reasonable excuse", with no known convictions recorded that year. Morality provisions covering cross-dressing, alcohol, eating during Ramadan and religious propagation were being enforced at that time, while the sharia implementing regulations had not yet been issued.

A person cannot change their name or gender marker on official documents, and sex reassignment surgery is not permitted. Trans visitors and residents therefore have no route to align identification with presentation, which leaves the mismatch visible to any official who inspects documents.

The wider code was completed on 3 April 2019, when stage three took effect. It prescribes death by stoning for anal sex and adultery, amputation for theft, and 40 strokes of the cane for sex between women; homosexuality had already been criminalised with penalties of up to ten years. The code applies principally to Muslims, roughly two-thirds of a population of about 420,000.

Sultan Hassanal Bolkiah announced in April 2019 that the country's moratorium on executions covers the new sharia provisions. Brunei has carried out no execution since 1957. The moratorium does not alter the non-capital penalties, which include caning and imprisonment, and does not repeal the cross-dressing offence.

LGBTI individuals in Brunei have reported intimidation by police, including threats to make their sexuality public, to obstruct access to government employment, or to block graduation from government academic institutions. Members of the community also report government monitoring of their activities and communications, and LGBTI-themed events have been refused permits under assembly and expression restrictions.
tangentialFactors:
The legal regime is backed by corporal punishment that applies where the highest evidentiary standards are not met: under the Syariah Penal Code Order, sex between men carries a maximum of seven years' imprisonment and thirty strokes of whipping, unmarried men one year in prison or 100 lashes, and sex between women any two of forty lashes of caning, up to ten years' imprisonment and a fine of up to B$40,000.

The Human Dignity Trust's April 2019 briefing and the UK House of Commons Library debate pack document the same stage-three package that drew condemnation from Human Rights Watch, which called it barbaric, and from the UN High Commissioner, who urged Brunei to halt implementation. Reporting at the time, including from TIME and France24, described a climate of fear among LGBTI Bruneians and noted that sources had no assurance of how the law would be applied to foreigners.

Bruneian society is reported to associate homosexuality with effeminate men, a social framing that raises the visibility risk for gender-nonconforming visitors independent of any arrest. Anyone convicted of "tarnishing the image of Islam" may be heavily punished. OutRight Action International has described Brunei as the country with the most worrisome state of LGBT rights in Southeast Asia.

For comparison, at least 67 countries worldwide criminalise same-sex relations and at least nine criminalise gender expression; Brunei is one of a very small number that write the cross-sex-presentation offence into national statute rather than sub-national law.
localsOnly:
Residents live under the full staged framework of the Syariah Penal Code Order 2013, with stage three in force since 3 April 2019 and the cross-dressing offence in section 198 available to prosecutors alongside the general morality provisions.

There is no legal pathway to amend name or gender on identification documents, and sex reassignment surgery is prohibited, so residents who transition socially do so without any documentary protection against the section 198 charge.

Government monitoring of LGBTI people's activities and communications, police intimidation including threatened outing, refusal of permits for LGBTI events, and discrimination reported in employment, housing, recreation and services shape daily life for residents in ways that fall more heavily on them than on short-term visitors.

The executed death penalty has been under a moratorium since 2019 and no execution has been carried out since 1957, but caning and imprisonment continue to be imposed.
outOfScopeNotes:
The full text of the Syariah Penal Code Order could not be retrieved at research time; the copy held in a Norwegian government archive returned an HTTP 403 error, so the exact wording of section 198 has been taken from secondary sources including the US State Department and Human Rights Watch rather than read in the statute itself.

An academic paper on the Brunei sharia penal code hosted on SSRN was likewise unavailable (HTTP 403) and has not contributed to this record.

No source in the inventory records enforcement of section 198 against a foreign visitor. The 2015 cross-dressing conviction involved a civil servant, a resident. Whether the offence has been applied to tourists since 2017, and how the sharia implementing regulations referred to as unissued in the 2017 report were subsequently framed, remain unresolved on the available sourcing.
